In this post we discuss some elements of the theory of surface conformal immersions in the language of quaternions. The principal motivation for this is from Keenan Crane's 2011 paper. The goal is to make myself more comfortable with this machinery, and to make sense of the principal result Theorem 3 in Kamberov et al.

1. The quaternions

The quaternions H {\mathbb{H}}H (H for its discoverer, William Hamilton), in Nathan Reed's own word, is like "complex numbers having eaten a super mushroom''. Formally, it is an associative division algebra over R {\mathbb{R}}R, with the following relation on the four basis vectors

i2=j2=k2=ijk=−1.\displaystyle i^{2}=j^{2}=k^{2}=ijk=-1.i2=j2=k2=ijk=−1.

Observe that the quaternionic multiplication is not commutative. We also see that a copy of complex numbers sits inside of it. The i,j,k {i,j,k}i,j,k part of a quaternion is called the imaginary part, and the space of imaginary part is denoted ImH {\text{Im}\mathbb{H}}ImH. The conjugate qˉ {\bar{q}}qˉ​ of a quaternion q {q}q has the negative of the imaginary part. The modulus ∣q∣ {|q|}∣q∣ of a quaternion q {q}q is equal to qˉq {\sqrt{\bar{q}q}}qˉ​q​.

It has been a long time since computer graphics people using quaternions, because of their close relation with the 3D rotations. Multiplying by a unit quaternion, either on the left or on the right, is a simultaneous rotation of two independent planes (2D subspaces), by the same angle. The difference of left and right multiplicatoin by the same quaternion is that one of the planes rotates in the opposite direction:

(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)=−x+iw−jz+ky,(w+ix+jy+kz)(i)=−x+iw+jz−ky.\displaystyle \begin{array}{rcl} (i)(w+ix+jy+kz) & = & -x+iw-jz+ky,\\ (w+ix+jy+kz)(i) & = & -x+iw+jz-ky. \end{array}(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(w+ix+jy+kz)(i)​==​−x+iw−jz+ky,−x+iw+jz−ky.​

Using this fact and the associativity, we can check the conjugation by quaternions results in a rotation that happens only for one plane:

(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(i−1)=(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(−i)=w+ix−jy−kz,\displaystyle (i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(i^{-1})=(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(-i)=w+ix-jy-kz,(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(i−1)=(i)(w+ix+jy+kz)(−i)=w+ix−jy−kz,

here wx {wx}wx rotation is canceled out and the yz {yz}yz rotation is done twice. In general,

Proposition 1 Conjugation by quaternions leave the imaginary subspace ImH≅R3 {\text{Im}\mathbb{H}\cong\mathbb{R}^{3}}ImH≅R3 invariant.

Proof: It is enough to see that if c∈R {c\in\mathbb{R}}c∈R, qcqˉ=c∣q∣2 {qc\bar{q}=c|q|^{2}}qcqˉ​=c∣q∣2 for all q∈H {q\in\mathbb{H}}q∈H. □ \Box□

This should be a first hint why quaternions are so intimatly related to 3D rotations, and in order to get , say a θ {\theta}θ-angled 3D rotaton that fixes some plane, aθ {\theta}θ-angled quaternion has to be applied twice (i.e. conjugation). We turn to these points next.

We will see that n=2 {n=2}n=2 . This means there exists a closed path in UT(S2) {UT(S^{2})}UT(S2) such that the unit tangent goes around twice the circle and yet the path is homotopically trivial. To see this, imagine in the above picture pulling the part behind the "twists'' to the front (there is nothing wrong if the annulus penetrates through itself while deforming). The usual annulus represents the situation that our hand runs around an axis only once. Hence we see that the group SO(3) {SO(3)}SO(3) has fundamental group Z2 {\mathbb{Z}_{2}}Z2​, and so it has a universal cover (which is a double covering), called Spin(3)≅SU(2) {Spin(3)\cong SU(2)}Spin(3)≅SU(2), which is then isomorphic to the unit quaternions (we won't prove these statements here, these can be found e.g. in Qiaochu's post). 3. Extrinsic Surface geoemtry in a new language

Since quaternions allow 3D rotations and uniform scaling to be represented as quaternionic conjugation, it is to be envisaged that they play an important part in the theory of conformal immersion of Riemann surfaces. From here we follow Kamberov et al.

4. Regular homotopy and spin transform

So far we only have local descriptions of a conformal immersion. To get a global theory we consider the results on the regular homotopy classes. Two immersions into R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3 of a given abstract surface is called regular homotopic if they can be connected by a continuous family of immersions. A regular homotopy class is denoted by [f] {[f]}[f]. Given a R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3 valued 1-form τ {\tau}τ, it is always possible to find a positive matrix valued function Aτ {A_{\tau}}Aτ​ such that the frame induced by τ {\tau}τ after compositing with Aτ {A_{\tau}}Aτ​ becomes the canonical frame on the immersed surface. Hirsch's theorem says that any continuous R3 {\mathbb{R}^{3}}R3 valued 1-form with rank two is homotopic to the differential df {df}df, thus the mapping τ↦Aτ {\tau\mapsto A_{\tau}}τ↦Aτ​ descends to a bijection [f]↦[Aτ]∈[M,SO(3)] {[f]\mapsto[A_{\tau}]\in[M,SO(3)]}[f]↦[Aτ​]∈[M,SO(3)], where the latter denotes the homotopy classes of SO(3) {SO(3)}SO(3) valued functions on M {M}M. By spin representation, the SO(3) {SO(3)}SO(3) valued function Aτ {A_{\tau}}Aτ​ on any loop can be lifted into the unit quaternions.
